questions.q: What is the safest way to size the blast radius of a new chaos experiment?
options: Always target 100% of production traffic so the result is unambiguous
Start with the smallest blast radius that still produces a useful answer, then widen it once that goes well
Blast radius doesn't matter as long as the kill switch works
Run the largest possible blast radius first to save time on repeat experiments
questions.explain: Starting small — one pod, a small traffic percentage — limits damage if the team's understanding of the system's resilience turns out to be wrong, and that understanding is exactly what the first run is testing.

questions.q: What makes a real abort criterion different from "we'll watch the dashboards and use our judgment"?
options: An abort criterion must be approved by a government regulator
There is no real difference; both are equally rigorous
An abort criterion only applies after the experiment has already finished
A real abort criterion is a specific, measurable, pre-agreed threshold that triggers an immediate stop without debate
questions.explain: "If checkout success rate drops below 97% for 60 seconds, abort" is unambiguous and decided in advance, so the person running the experiment can act without arguing over whether it's bad enough yet.

questions.q: Why does real chaos engineering practice run experiments during business hours with the team watching, rather than as a surprise overnight test?
options: Because controlling when the experiment runs and having people ready to intervene is what makes it safe, rather than just an unplanned outage someone scheduled
Because chaos engineering tools only function during business hours
Because engineers are legally required to be awake during any production change
Because business-hours testing produces fake results that don't reflect real conditions
questions.explain: An unmonitored 3 a.m. test removes the safety benefit of the practice — it becomes indistinguishable from an unplanned incident, just one you caused yourself.

questions.q: In the Chaos Mesh PodChaos example from this lesson, what does `mode: one` control?
options: The total duration of the experiment in seconds
Which Kubernetes namespace the controller is allowed to run in
The blast radius — it kills exactly one matching pod rather than every pod matching the selector
Whether the experiment runs in staging instead of production
questions.explain: `mode: one` is the control that limits the action to a single matching pod, keeping the blast radius small instead of affecting every pod with that label.

questions.q: What is the correct relationship between a tool like Gremlin or Chaos Mesh and the safety discipline described in this lesson?
options: The tool replaces the need for abort criteria, since it halts automatically without configuration
The tool is the mechanism that executes the practice precisely and stoppably; the safety discipline (blast radius, abort criteria, people watching) still has to be decided by the team
The tool and the safety discipline are unrelated to each other
Using a dedicated tool means business-hours monitoring is no longer necessary
questions.explain: Gremlin and Chaos Mesh make it easy to inject a precise, scoped failure and stop it — but the blast radius, abort criteria, and decision to have people watching are judgment calls the team still has to make.
